newsitem.title: USA: St Louis Fed economist warns stock market cyclical.
newsitem.headline: St Louis Fed economist warns stock market cyclical.

text.p: The U.S stock market is vulnerable to lengthy bear cycles that follow spectacular bull runs and that reflects a shift in investors' willingness to take risk, a Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis economist said.
"The current bull market is a far, far better thing than we are bound to experience when the next bear market arrives," St. Louis Fed economist William Emmons told Reuters.
A summary of Emmons' research on U.S. stock performance, "A Tale of Two Cycles," will appear in the St. Louis Fed's April issue of "Monetary Trends."

The current bull run, that started on August 12, 1982 when the Dow Jones industrial average closed at 777, propelled the index to a record closing high of 7085.16 two days ago -- or a 15-percent average gain over the past 15 years.
The rate of appreciation in the two years preceeding that record was a whopping 28.3 percent.

"Both the last two years and the 15-year bull market of which we are part show stock price increases far above their long-run historical average growth rate which, from 1900 to 1997, has been just under 5.0 percent annually," Emmons noted.
Emmons said the common denominator of all major trend reversals is a profound change in investors' risk tolerance.
"Investors expect some rate of return, including capital gains and dividends, that compensate them for the risk they are taking," the St. Louis Fed economist said.

"The last two years have been more than anyone but the extreme optimists would have expected," added Emmons who explained that investors' willingness to take risks is generally a function of the expected rate of return.

A "wealth effect," or stockholders' willingness to spend more on the basis of paper gains, may boost consumer spending and growth beyond sustainable trends. The latest breath-taking bull run, however, does not seem to have affected growth yet.
"Looking at the past two years, there has been a lot of unexpected wealth gains. This very rapid run-up does not seem to translate into wealth yet because it has been so unexpected," Emmons admitted.
The opposite outcome of rapid stock gains may be a sudden market correction that sets a negative psychology for consumers and may unexpectedly throw the economy into a downturn.
"My personal feeling would be that a sharp market correction could hurt the economy through reduced consumer confidence. It's a very complicated cause-and-effect situation," Emmons added.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan cautioned against potential imbalances, whatever their source may be, in his recent Congressional testimony.
Emmons further made the point that the impact of market crashes may highly vary, depending on their cause, and is not a function of the steepness of the correction.

"A perfect example is the 1987 crash which was an example of a technical crash. The crash was heard around the world but there was no fundamental reason anywhere to cause it," said Emmons who explained the magnitude of the plunge by technical problems between major U.S. exchanges.

In contrast, Emmons said the mini-crash of 1989 was more telling of a fundamental problem in the U.S. economy because it exposed the thrift industry crisis and major banking sector problems tied to poor balance sheets and inflated real estate prices.

"It is useful to recall that both of the previous major bull markets in this century were followed by extended periods of very poor stock performance," said Emmons, referring to the stock bull runs of October 1923-September 1929, and April 1942-January 1966.
Emmons said the annualized compounded rate of increase was 25 percent in that first bull run and 10 percent in the latter.

Even if a market holds at record levels, it would no longer post fresh capital gains and leave stockholders with no other return but the stock dividends -- currently just 2.0 percent -- which means a minor stock price correction would leave them with no return at all on their investments in the near future.
Emmons said the implications for the economy of a sharp market appreciation are two-fold.
